title: After original sin remitted, material fomes/concupiscence remains
source_text: XXIX. Praesertim vero remisso per gratiam justificantem peccato originali, agnoscunt nihilominus in justificatis manere id quod in hoc peccato materiale vocant, nempe, pronitatem ad malum, & difficultatem in bono, & quandam, ut loquuntur, deordinationem & perversitatem naturae contra ordinem in prima creatione positum. Qua deordinatione fit ut inferiores animae facultates pronae sint ad resistendum & rebellandum rationi, atque legi divinae, totusque homo sit ad malum proclivis, & magnam in bene agendo difficultatem sentiat. Et ista ad malum pronitas & naturae depravatio, est id quod vulgo in Scholis concupiscentia & fomes appellatur.
pass_a_gloss: Especially when original sin has been remitted by justifying grace, they nevertheless acknowledge that there remains in the justified what they call the material in this sin, namely a proneness to evil and difficulty in good, and a certain, as they speak, disorder and perversity of nature against the order set in the first creation. By which disorder it happens that the lower faculties of the soul are prone to resist and rebel against reason and the divine law, and the whole man is inclined to evil and feels great difficulty in doing well. And that proneness to evil and depravation of nature is what is commonly called in the Schools concupiscence and fomes.
pass_b_english: Even after original sin's remission, Rome keeps the 'material'—proneness to evil, difficulty in good, nature's disorder.
That is scholastic concupiscence or fomes: lower powers rebel; the whole man tilts to evil.
